item.title: ToddyCat Umbrij Hits Gmail; CVE-2026-20230 and CVE-2026-45659 Exploited
item.content:encoded:
Cisco finally confirms attackers exploiting Unified CM flaw — Must Read

Cisco confirmed that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-20230, an SSRF flaw in Unified Communications Manager that can be abused via crafted HTTP requests. Customers should urgently upgrade to fixed releases or disable the vulnerable WebDialer service until patches can be applied.

  • Cisco confirmed that attackers are actively exploiting CVE-2026-20230, a Unified Communications Manager vulnerability patched in early June.
  • CVE-2026-20230 can be exploited remotely by unauthenticated attackers in low-complexity server-side request forgery attacks using a crafted HTTP request.
  • Defused reported on June 22 that attackers had begun exploiting the flaw with properly constructed file:// payloads to create files on targeted devices.
  • Cisco urged customers to upgrade to fixed Unified CM releases and advised those unable to patch immediately to disable the vulnerable WebDialer service.
  • Shadowserver is tracking over 200 Cisco Unified CM instances exposed online, mostly in Asia and North America.

CISA: Microsoft SharePoint RCE flaw now actively exploited — Must Read

CISA says attackers are now actively exploiting CVE-2026-45659, a Microsoft SharePoint remote code execution flaw that lets low-privileged authenticated users run code on unpatched servers. Federal agencies have been ordered to patch by Saturday, and exposed SharePoint servers should be secured immediately.

  • CISA warned that attackers have begun exploiting CVE-2026-45659, a high-severity Microsoft SharePoint remote code execution vulnerability.
  • Microsoft says any authenticated attacker with at least Site Member permissions can exploit the flaw over the network to remotely execute code on a SharePoint Server.
  • Microsoft released security updates for SharePoint Enterprise Server 2016, SharePoint Server 2019, and SharePoint Server Subscription Edition on May 21 after the CVE was accidentally omitted from the May 2026 Security Updates.
  • Shadowserver is tracking more than 10,000 Microsoft SharePoint servers exposed online, but the article says it is unknown how many have been secured against CVE-2026-45659 attacks.
  • CISA added CVE-2026-45659 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog and ordered Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies to secure their servers by Saturday under BOD 26-04.

ToddyCat-Linked Umbrij Malware Abuses OAuth to Access Gmail via Google API — Must Read

Kaspersky says the ToddyCat APT is using a new .NET malware called Umbrij to hijack active Gmail sessions in Chromium-based browsers, obtain OAuth authorization codes via remote debugging, and access corporate email through Google APIs. Organizations should review and revoke suspicious Google Workspace Migration/Sync app access if those tools are not in legitimate use.

  • Kaspersky attributed a new malware called Umbrij to the threat actor ToddyCat, describing it as a tool designed to gain covert access to victims’ Gmail-hosted corporate email through the Google API.
  • Umbrij exploits an active Gmail session in Chromium-based browsers by launching Chrome or Edge in headless mode, connecting through a remote debugging port, obtaining an OAuth authorization code, and exchanging it for an access token.
  • Kaspersky said it discovered Umbrij during threat hunting after a scheduled task impersonating its software launched a digitally signed file that used DLL side-loading to load the Umbrij DLL.
  • The malware copies selected Chrome or Edge profile data into backup folders, uses the copied profiles to preserve active user cookies, and automates browser actions with Puppeteer to grant permissions to Google Workspace migration-related applications.
  • Kaspersky advised organizations to review Google account application connections for “Google Workspace Migration for Microsoft Outlook” or “Google Workspace Sync for Microsoft Outlook” and revoke access if those applications are not legitimately used.

Field reports from Patch the Planet — Should Read

Trail of Bits says OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber autonomously built a sophisticated fuzzing campaign for zlib in about a day, showing that advanced models can now perform security research work that once required significant expert time. The key takeaway is that maintainers need to proactively use similar tooling and strict validation rules before attackers do.

  • Trail of Bits is running Patch the Planet with OpenAI to pair its engineers with more than 30 open-source projects and find security bugs before highly capable models create large volumes of bug reports for maintainers.
  • In one Patch the Planet field report, GPT-5.5-Cyber built a custom fuzzing campaign for zlib in a single day, including harnesses across a dozen entrypoints, sanitizer and variant builds, seeds, and multiple findings under coordinated disclosure.
  • GPT-5.5-Cyber decided that dynamic fuzz testing was a higher-value path than static source review for zlib and used the Codex /goal command to maintain the objective across multiple turns.
  • The model used ASan and UBSan builds, repurposed existing edge-case tests for fuzz seeds, wrote C/C++ harnesses for multiple zlib entrypoints, and used compile-time variants such as INFLATE_STRICT, BUILDFIXED, and PKZIP_BUG_WORKAROUND.
  • The article says bespoke fuzzing is no longer out of reach for low-skill attackers or limited to mature projects, so maintainers of security-critical code should run this kind of testing first with strict validity rules.

One Hyphen From Trusted: A Lookalike-Domain Vendor Impersonation That Beat the Eye and the Authentication Stack — May Read

Attackers impersonated a known supplier by registering a one-hyphen lookalike domain and sending authenticated email that passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, showing that authentication alone cannot detect vendor impersonation. The key defense was behavioral relationship analysis that noticed a familiar contact name coming from a new, suspicious domain.

  • An attacker registered lookalike domains for a known supplier, including a hyphenated near-miss used as the sending and reply-to domain and another variant used to mirror the known contact's identity.
  • The email used the exact display name of a supplier contact the recipient had corresponded with before and presented a routine sales pitch about lowering beveling costs.
  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all passed because the attacker owned the lookalike sending domain and sent the message through a Gmail-API sales-engagement tool, while the domain's DMARC policy was set to p=none.
  • The email contained a link whose displayed text mimicked the lookalike domain while the actual destination pointed elsewhere, and link scanning flagged this mismatch as malicious.
  • The article says the message was caught by relationship analysis that recognized the known contact name was arriving from a domain the contact had never used before.

Opera rolls out Paste Protect feature to fight ClickFix attacks — May Read

Opera has rolled out Paste Protect, a default-on browser feature that blocks suspicious commands from being copied to the clipboard to help stop ClickFix social-engineering attacks. Users are warned when risky clipboard content is detected and can review or allow trusted sites if needed.

  • Opera introduced Paste Protect, a security feature designed to block ClickFix-style attacks that trick users into copying and executing malicious commands.
  • ClickFix attacks commonly use fake verification processes or problem-fixing instructions to make victims run dangerous commands with their own user privileges, often leading to information-stealer malware.
  • Paste Protect combines Opera’s existing Hijack protection with a new Injection protection component that blocks potentially harmful commands before they reach the clipboard.
  • Opera says Paste Protect uses platform-specific detection rules for Windows, macOS, and Linux to scan copied content for patterns associated with malicious scripts and commands.
  • When suspicious clipboard content is detected, Opera blocks the copy action, shows a warning and red address-bar indicator, and lets users review the first 120 characters before approving the copy after a 5-second timeout.

Microsoft fixes bug that removed Copilot buttons in Outlook — May Read

Microsoft fixed a Classic Outlook bug that caused Copilot Chat or Copilot buttons to disappear for Windows users with Copilot Chat Basic licenses. Users still affected should restart Outlook or update to the latest build, with rollback or Outlook on the web as workarounds.

  • Microsoft fixed a known issue that caused Copilot Chat or Copilot buttons in Classic Outlook to disappear for Windows users with the Copilot Chat Basic license.
  • Affected users may have seen the Copilot button missing above the ribbon, the Copilot icon missing from the left app bar or More Apps area, or Copilot commands appearing unavailable or not opening.
  • Microsoft said the Outlook Team addressed the issue with a service change on June 29, 2026, and advised users who still cannot see the buttons to restart Classic Outlook.
  • Affected customers are also advised to update to the latest build through File, Office Account, Update Options, and Update Now.
  • Users who cannot upgrade can work around the issue by reverting to Current Channel build 16.0.20026.20168 or using the new Outlook or Outlook Web Access.

The 2026 Verizon DBIR Stopped Asking How Attackers Get in and Started Asking Where They Go — Optional

The 2026 Verizon DBIR suggests that while vulnerability exploitation is now the top initial access vector, most privilege escalation happens through permissions, configurations, and trust relationships rather than patchable flaws. The key takeaway is that organizations need attack graph visibility and privilege management to cut off escalation paths, not just faster patching.

  • The 2026 Verizon DBIR found that exploitation of vulnerabilities became the top initial access vector at 31% of breaches, up from 20% the previous year.
  • Verizon’s attack graph analysis found that 16% of organizations had about 80% exposure, meaning attackers with low-level privileges had an 80% or better chance of reaching a key administrative account.
  • The article states that 83% of privilege escalation incidents involve no vulnerability, and that privilege management covers 65% of escalation mitigation techniques.
  • Verizon modeled real environments as graphs of users, groups, permissions, and trust relationships to trace possible attacker paths from an initial foothold to high-level access.
  • The DBIR found that only 26% of CISA KEV vulnerabilities were fully remediated in 2025, with median time to full resolution rising to 43 days.

Identity Lifecycle Management Wasn't Built for AI Agents — Optional

Traditional identity lifecycle management is built around HR-driven human events like hiring, role changes, and termination, so it misses AI agents that are created, modified, and retired through deployment pipelines. Organizations need continuous discovery, behavioral monitoring, owner attribution, and operational-status-based deprovisioning to govern agent identities and credentials effectively.

  • Traditional identity lifecycle management is built around human employment events such as joining, changing roles, and leaving, with HR systems acting as the authoritative source for provisioning and deprovisioning access.
  • AI agents fall outside this model because they are often created by developers, orchestration frameworks, or deployment pipelines rather than HR systems, and they may receive credentials without an IGA workflow or defined identity owner.
  • AI agents can expand their access at runtime through tool-calling, retrieval patterns, API use, and multi-environment instantiation, while traditional IGA tools may only see them as static service accounts or API credentials.
  • Agent identities often do not trigger access reviews or offboarding events, which can leave stale service accounts, API keys, and OAuth grants active after the related workload is retired.
  • The article recommends extending identity lifecycle management for agents through continuous discovery, agent-specific attribute modeling, policy-driven provisioning, behavioral monitoring, and deprecation workflows based on operational status.

Enrich Your Palo Alto XSOAR Environment with Silent Push Threat Check API — Optional

Silent Push is promoting its Threat Check API integration for Palo Alto XSOAR, enabling on-demand threat intelligence lookups and automated workflows for domains, IPs, nameservers, and IOFA feeds. The tool is available to try through Silent Push’s free Community Edition.

  • Silent Push has an integration for Palo Alto XSOAR that adds Silent Push threat intelligence capabilities to the environment.
  • The integration enables on-demand lookups and automated workflows for domains, IP addresses, nameservers, and Indicators of Future Attack feeds.
  • The integration is intended to streamline incident response and threat hunting.
  • Silent Push says the tool can be tried using its free Community Edition.
  • The article invites readers to sign up and share feedback on the tool.

Investigating a Phishing Campaign: How to Uncover Malicious Domains with Silent Push — Optional

Silent Push published a hands-on walkthrough showing how analysts can investigate phishing campaigns and uncover malicious domains using its platform. The article mainly promotes trying the tool through its free Community Edition.

  • The article presents a hands-on walkthrough about investigating phishing campaigns.
  • The walkthrough explains how to uncover malicious domains using Silent Push.
  • The article says the walkthrough is intended for threat hunters, SOC analysts, incident responders, and curious readers.
  • The article describes the walkthrough as offering practical insight into modern, preemptive threat detection.
  • The article invites readers to try Silent Push through its free Community Edition.

Quick Pivots: SSDEEP and HTML Content Similarity — Optional

Silent Push is promoting its HTML Content Similarity Search, which uses SSDEEP-style similarity to help find malicious sites that reuse HTML templates without requiring scripting or complex workflows.

  • Threat actors reuse HTML templates to create malicious sites at scale.
  • Traditionally, finding malicious sites that reuse HTML templates required a complex, multi-step process and scripting skills.
  • HTML Content Similarity Search is presented as a simpler way to find these sites.
  • The tool provides deduplicated, high-relevance results without requiring coding.
  • Silent Push says the tool can be tried using its free Community Edition.
